mainEntity.name: What is a package in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A package in Java is a namespace that groups related classes, interfaces, enumerations, and annotations together. It serves two key purposes: organization (related types are stored together, making large codebases navigable) and access control (package-private visibility restricts access to only classes in the same package). Packages map directly to directory structures on disk — a class in package com.example.service must physically reside in a com/example/service/ directory. The package declaration must be the very first statement in a Java source file (before imports and class declaration): package com.example.service; Every Java program is in a package — if no package is declared, the class belongs to the unnamed default package, which is fine for small experiments but unsuitable for production code.

The Java API (Application Programming Interface) is the collection of pre-written classes, interfaces, and packages that ship with every Java installation as part of the Java Standard Library (also called the Java Class Library or JCL). It provides ready-to-use implementations for common programming tasks: data structures (java.util), input/output (java.io, java.nio), networking (java.net), mathematics (java.math), string manipulation (java.lang), date/time handling (java.time), concurrency (java.util.concurrent), and much more. Using the Java API means you do not have to implement fundamental operations from scratch — you import the needed package and use battle-tested, optimized, and well-documented classes. The full Java API documentation is available at docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between import and package in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: The package statement and import statement serve different purposes. package declares which package the current class BELONGS TO — it defines the class's address in the Java namespace. There can be only one package declaration per file and it must be the first statement. import makes classes from OTHER packages available in the current file by their simple name — without import, you must use the fully qualified class name (e.g., java.util.ArrayList) every time. import does not copy or include code — it is purely a compile-time shortcut that tells the compiler where to look for a type name. java.lang is the only package that is automatically imported — all other packages require explicit import statements.

mainEntity.name: What is a wildcard import in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: A wildcard import uses an asterisk (*) to import all public types from a package in one statement: import java.util.*; — this makes all public classes in java.util (ArrayList, HashMap, Scanner, etc.) available by their simple names. Wildcard imports do NOT import sub-packages — import java.util.* does NOT import java.util.concurrent.*. They also do NOT affect performance at runtime — the Java compiler resolves exactly which classes are used and only includes those. The debate: wildcard imports are concise but can cause ambiguity when two packages have classes with the same name (e.g., java.util.Date and java.sql.Date). Specific imports are preferred in professional code for clarity and IDE navigation.

mainEntity.name: Which Java package is imported automatically?

acceptedAnswer.text: The java.lang package is the only package that Java imports automatically into every source file — you never need to write import java.lang.*; explicitly. It contains the most fundamental classes in Java: String, Integer, Long, Double, Boolean, Math, Object, System, StringBuilder, Thread, Runnable, Exception, RuntimeException, NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, and more. All other packages — including java.util, java.io, java.net, java.time, java.math, and every third-party library — must be explicitly imported. This is why you can use String and System.out.println() without any import statement, but must import Scanner, ArrayList, and LocalDate.

sections.title: What is a Package in Java?

blocks.text: A package in Java is a namespace mechanism that groups related classes, interfaces, enumerations, and annotations into a single logical unit. Think of it as a folder system for your Java code — just as you organize files into folders on your computer, you organize Java types into packages. Packages solve two fundamental problems that arise in large projects: name collision (two classes with the same name in different packages coexist peacefully) and controlled access (package-private members are only visible within the same package).

Packages in Java are directly mapped to the directory structure on disk. A class declared in package com.techsustainify.service must physically reside in a directory path com/techsustainify/service/ relative to the source root. This one-to-one mapping between packages and directories is enforced by the Java compiler — if the directory structure does not match the package declaration, the code will not compile.

The Java API (Application Programming Interface) is the massive collection of pre-built packages and classes that ship with every Java installation — the Java Standard Library. It provides thousands of ready-to-use classes for collections, I/O, networking, math, concurrency, date/time, and much more. Learning which packages exist in the Java API and what they contain is one of the most practical skills a Java developer can develop.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Packages & API at a Glance
blocks.text: Package = namespace that groups related classes + maps to directory structure on disk. package statement must be the FIRST statement in a Java file (before imports, before class). import makes class names from other packages available without full qualification. java.lang is the ONLY package auto-imported — all others require explicit import. Wildcard import (import java.util.*;) imports all public types in a package — not sub-packages. Static import allows using static members without class name prefix. User-defined packages follow reverse domain naming: com.companyname.module. Access modifier + package: package-private (no modifier) = visible only within same package. Java API key packages: java.lang, java.util, java.io, java.math, java.time, java.net, java.util.concurrent.

The package statement declares which package a Java source file belongs to. It must be the absolute first statement in the file — before any import statements, before any class declarations, and before any comments (though comments above the package statement are technically allowed). Only one package statement is permitted per source file.

items.title: Package Declaration Syntax & Rules
Package-to-Directory Mapping
items.text: Java enforces a strict one-to-one mapping between package names and directory structure. Package: com.techsustainify.model → Directory: src/com/techsustainify/model/. The Java compiler (javac) and classloader use this mapping to locate class files. If EmployeeService.java declares package com.techsustainify.service; but is saved in the wrong directory, the compiler produces: error: class EmployeeService is public, should be declared in a file named EmployeeService.java. Modern IDEs (IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, VS Code) enforce this automatically — creating a class in a package auto-creates the matching directory structure.

items.title: Naming Conventions — Reverse Domain
items.text: The standard Java convention for package names is reverse Internet domain notation: com.companyname.projectname.module. Examples: com.google.gson (Google's Gson library), org.springframework.boot (Spring Boot), io.micrometer.core (Micrometer metrics), com.techsustainify.tutorial. Why reverse domain? It guarantees global uniqueness — two companies with different domains cannot produce a package name collision. Rules: all lowercase, no hyphens (use underscores if necessary), avoid Java keywords as package name segments. Segments beginning with digits are technically invalid Java identifiers — a leading underscore is the workaround: com.example._123module.

blocks.title: 💡 How to Explore the Java API
blocks.text: The official Java API documentation (Javadoc) is your best friend. Bookmark it: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/. Every class, method, parameter, return type, and exception is documented with examples. In IntelliJ IDEA: Ctrl+Click on any class name to jump to its source. Ctrl+Q shows quick Javadoc. In Eclipse: hover over a class name to see its documentation. The habit of reading the official Javadoc before writing utility code — to check if Java already has it — is what separates professional developers from beginners.

java.lang is the only Java package that is automatically imported into every Java source file. It contains the absolute bedrock of the Java language — classes so fundamental that Java programs cannot function without them. You use java.lang classes constantly without realizing it: every time you declare a String, call System.out.println(), use Math.abs(), catch a NullPointerException, or create a Thread.

sections.title: java.time — The Modern Date & Time API

blocks.text: The java.time package (introduced in Java 8, JSR-310) is the definitive replacement for the legacy java.util.Date and Calendar classes, which were notoriously confusing, mutable, and poorly designed. java.time provides an immutable, thread-safe, and richly expressive API for dates, times, durations, periods, and time zones. In all new Java code, always use java.time — never java.util.Date or java.util.Calendar.

sections.title: User-Defined Packages — Structuring Your Own Code

blocks.text: Beyond using the Java API, you will create your own packages to organize your application's source code. A well-designed package structure reflects your application's architecture — it groups classes by their responsibility and layer, makes navigation intuitive, and controls what is visible across package boundaries.

items.title: Common Package Structures in Production
items.text: Layer-based (traditional): com.company.app.model, com.company.app.service, com.company.app.repository, com.company.app.controller, com.company.app.util, com.company.app.exception. Feature-based (modern, preferred for large systems): com.company.app.employee, com.company.app.payroll, com.company.app.reporting — each feature package contains its own model, service, repository, and controller. The feature-based structure is favored in microservices and domain-driven design because each feature's code is co-located and can be independently extracted into a separate service.

items.title: Sub-Packages — Not Inherited
items.text: Java packages are NOT hierarchical in terms of access — a sub-package does NOT have special access to its parent package. com.example.app and com.example.app.service are completely separate, independent packages. Package-private members in com.example.app are NOT visible in com.example.app.service — only public and protected members (with inheritance) are accessible. This surprises many beginners who assume sub-packages can access parent package internals. Each package is a completely isolated namespace — only the naming convention (dots) creates the visual hierarchy; there is no actual inheritance of access rights.

items.title: Compiling and Running with Packages
items.text: Compiling: javac -d out src/com/techsustainify/model/Employee.java — the -d flag specifies the output directory root; javac creates the matching subdirectory structure automatically. Running: java -cp out com.techsustainify.Main — the fully qualified class name (package + class) is required. With multiple source files: javac -d out src/**/*.java or use a build tool (Maven, Gradle) which handles compilation, packaging, and dependency management automatically. In practice, you will almost always use a build tool — manual javac commands are for learning purposes only.

sections.title: Static Import — Using Static Members Without Class Prefix

blocks.text: Static import (introduced in Java 5) allows you to import static methods and fields directly, so they can be used without qualifying them with the class name. It is most useful for heavily used constants like Math.PI, test assertions like Assertions.assertEquals, and factory methods. Use it judiciously — overuse makes code confusing because readers cannot tell which class a static member belongs to.

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These anti-patterns represent common misuses of packages and the Java API in professional code. Each one either causes maintenance problems, correctness bugs, or signals poor understanding of Java's design.

items.title: Putting Everything in the Default Package
items.text: Placing all classes in the unnamed default package (no package declaration) is fine for tiny experiments but unacceptable in any real project. It makes classes impossible to import from other packages, prevents proper access control, causes IDE navigation chaos, and signals no understanding of Java project structure. Every production Java class must be in a named package following the reverse domain convention. Build tools like Maven and Gradle will also not package default-package classes correctly in JARs.

items.title: Wildcard Imports in Production Code
items.text: import java.util.*; is convenient during development but is rejected in most professional codebases and style guides (Google Java Style: specific imports only). Wildcard imports hide which classes are actually used, can cause silent ambiguity when two packages share a class name, and make code navigation harder — you cannot Ctrl+Click an import to jump to the class. Enable 'Optimize Imports' in your IDE to auto-manage specific imports. The one exception: test code with import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.* is widely accepted because all assertions clearly belong to JUnit.

items.title: Using double/float for Financial Calculations
items.text: Using primitive double or float for any monetary amount — price, tax, discount, interest rate, total — is a critical correctness bug, not just a code smell. IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is FALSE in Java. For all financial and currency arithmetic, use java.math.BigDecimal with String constructor and explicit RoundingMode. ALWAYS: new BigDecimal("19.99") — NEVER: new BigDecimal(19.99). Passing a double to BigDecimal's double constructor defeats the purpose entirely.

items.title: Using java.util.Date or Calendar in New Code
items.text: java.util.Date and java.util.Calendar are deprecated in spirit — they are mutable, poorly designed, non-thread-safe, and confusing (months in Calendar are 0-based). Since Java 8, the java.time package provides everything you need — immutably, thread-safely, and expressively. New code should use LocalDate, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, Duration, Period, and DateTimeFormatter exclusively. If you encounter a legacy API requiring java.util.Date, use the conversion methods: Date.from(instant) and date.toInstant(). Code reviews should reject any new java.util.Date usage.

items.title: God Package — Dumping All Classes in One Package
items.text: Putting all classes in a single package (e.g., com.company.app with 100+ classes) eliminates the organizational and access-control benefits of packages entirely. It is the package equivalent of a 10,000-line God class. Split by layer (model, service, repository, controller) or by feature (user, product, order, payment). A good rule of thumb: if a package contains more than 15-20 classes, consider splitting it. Package structure should reflect your architecture — if your architecture is well-designed, your package structure will be naturally modular.

items.title: Overusing Static Import
items.text: Static import of non-obvious static members makes code cryptic. When a reader sees processOrder(id) in your code, they have no idea which class it belongs to — they must search the imports or hover with an IDE. This slows comprehension and makes bugs harder to spot. Reserve static import for: universally known constants (PI, E, MAX_VALUE), test assertion methods (assertEquals, assertTrue in JUnit files), and factory/builder methods where the class name is obvious from context. Never static-import business logic methods or domain-specific utility methods.

sections.title: Java Packages & API Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: Package and API questions test your understanding of Java's namespace system, visibility rules, the standard library, and practical use of key API classes. These appear consistently in Java interviews at all experience levels.

items.q: Q1. What is a package in Java? Why is it used?
items.a: A package in Java is a namespace that groups related classes, interfaces, enumerations, and annotations together. It serves three key purposes: (1) Organization — related types are stored together, making large codebases navigable and maintainable. (2) Name collision prevention — two classes with the same name (e.g., Date in java.util and java.sql) can coexist in separate packages without conflict. (3) Access control — the package-private access level (no modifier) restricts visibility to classes in the same package, enabling strong encapsulation. Packages map directly to directory structures — com.example.service maps to com/example/service/ on disk.

items.q: Q2. Which package is imported automatically in every Java program?
items.a: java.lang is the only package automatically imported into every Java source file — you never need to write import java.lang.*. It contains the most fundamental Java classes: String, Integer, Long, Double, Boolean, Character, Byte, Short, Float — all primitive wrapper classes. Also: Math, Object, System, StringBuilder, StringBuffer, Thread, Runnable, Exception, RuntimeException, Error, NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, IndexOutOfBoundsException, ClassCastException, and many more. This is why you can use String and System.out.println() without any import statement — they are in java.lang. All other packages, including java.util, java.io, java.time, and all third-party libraries, require explicit import.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between import java.util.ArrayList and import java.util.*?
items.a: import java.util.ArrayList is a single-type import — it imports exactly one class (ArrayList) from java.util. import java.util.* is a wildcard (on-demand) import — it imports all public types in java.util (ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet, LinkedList, Collections, Arrays, Scanner, Optional, etc.). Key facts about wildcard import: (1) It does NOT import sub-packages — import java.util.* does NOT import java.util.concurrent.* or java.util.function.*. (2) It does NOT affect performance — the compiler resolves only actually-used classes. (3) It can cause ambiguity — if java.util and java.sql both have a Date class and both are wildcard-imported, Date becomes ambiguous. Single-type imports are preferred in professional code for clarity and to avoid ambiguity.

items.q: Q4. What is package-private (default) access in Java?
items.a: Package-private (no access modifier) is Java's fourth access level — used when NO modifier is written before a class, field, method, or constructor. A package-private member is visible ONLY to classes in the SAME package. Classes in other packages — even sub-packages — cannot access it. Example: if class QueryEngine in com.example.engine has a package-private method buildPlan(), then QueryOptimizer in the same package can call it, but QueryController in com.example.api cannot. Package-private is the strongest encapsulation after private — it is a powerful tool for hiding implementation details within a package while exposing only the public API. It is Java's way of creating 'internal-to-package' APIs.

items.q: Q5. Why should you never use double for financial calculations? What is the alternative?
items.a: double uses IEEE 754 binary floating-point representation, which cannot exactly represent most decimal fractions. 0.1 + 0.2 in double gives 0.30000000000000004, not 0.3. In financial calculations, these tiny errors accumulate across thousands of transactions and produce incorrect totals, taxes, and balances — a serious business bug. The correct alternative is java.math.BigDecimal, which stores decimal numbers exactly. Critical rules: (1) Always use the String constructor — new BigDecimal("0.1") is exact; new BigDecimal(0.1) inherits the double's imprecision. (2) Always specify RoundingMode explicitly — HALF_UP for financial rounding. (3) Use setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP) for monetary values to ensure consistent 2 decimal places.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between java.util.Date and java.time.LocalDate?
items.a: java.util.Date (pre-Java 8): mutable (dangerous in multithreaded code), represents both date and time in a single object, months are zero-indexed (January = 0), does not handle timezones cleanly, poorly designed API, mostly deprecated methods. java.time.LocalDate (Java 8+, JSR-310): immutable and thread-safe, represents ONLY a date (no time, no timezone), months are 1-indexed (January = 1), rich, expressive API with plus/minus operations, formatting, comparison, period calculation. The java.time package completely replaces java.util.Date and Calendar for new code. Use LocalDate for dates only, LocalDateTime for date+time without timezone, ZonedDateTime for timezone-aware date+time. Convert legacy Date to LocalDate via: date.toInstant().atZone(ZoneId.systemDefault()).toLocalDate().

items.q: Q7. Can a sub-package access the package-private members of its parent package?
items.a: NO — sub-packages have NO special access to parent package members in Java. com.example.app and com.example.app.service are completely independent, isolated packages. The dot-separated naming convention creates only a visual hierarchy — there is no actual inheritance of access rights. Package-private members in com.example.app are accessible ONLY within com.example.app — NOT from com.example.app.service, not from com.example, not from anywhere outside. This surprises developers who assume Java packages work like directory permissions. If you need a class in a sub-package to access something in the parent package, you must make that member public (or protected if inheritance is involved) — there is no intermediate visibility level.

items.q: Q8. What is static import? When should and should not you use it?
items.a: Static import (import static) allows using static methods and fields directly without the class name prefix. Example: import static java.lang.Math.PI; — then use PI directly instead of Math.PI. USE static import for: (1) Universally recognized constants — PI, E, MAX_VALUE. (2) JUnit test assertions — import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*; allows assertEquals() directly. (3) Enum values used repeatedly — import static com.example.Status.*; to use ACTIVE instead of Status.ACTIVE. DO NOT use static import for: (1) Business logic utility methods — readers cannot tell which class they belong to. (2) Generic names — if multiple classes have a static method named format(), imports would clash. (3) Overused in non-test code — it makes the codebase harder to understand and navigate.

items.q: Q9. What happens if you have import java.util.* and import java.sql.* and use Date?
items.a: Both java.util.Date and java.sql.Date exist. When you write import java.util.* and import java.sql.*, both packages are on-demand-imported. If you then write Date d = new Date(); in your code, the Java compiler cannot determine which Date you mean — both are available through the wildcard imports. It reports a compile-time error: 'reference to Date is ambiguous.' The fix: use the fully qualified class name for whichever (or both) you need: java.util.Date utilDate = new java.util.Date(); java.sql.Date sqlDate = new java.sql.Date(...);. This is one reason professional code prefers single-type imports over wildcard imports — single-type imports make this conflict immediately visible and force you to resolve it explicitly.

items.q: Q10. What are some of the most important packages in the Java API and what do they contain?
items.a: The most important Java API packages: java.lang (auto-imported): String, Math, Integer, System, Object, Thread, Exception. java.util: ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet, LinkedList, TreeMap, Collections, Arrays, Scanner, Optional, UUID, Random. java.util.concurrent: ExecutorService, Executors, ConcurrentHashMap, Future, CountDownLatch, Semaphore. java.util.stream: Stream, Collectors, IntStream — for functional-style collection processing. java.io: File, BufferedReader, PrintWriter, InputStream, OutputStream, Serializable. java.nio.file: Path, Paths, Files — modern file API (use instead of java.io.File). java.math: BigDecimal, BigInteger — for precise arithmetic. java.time: LocalDate, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime, Duration, Period, DateTimeFormatter — modern date/time. java.sql: Connection, PreparedStatement, ResultSet — for JDBC database connectivity. java.net: URL, HttpURLConnection, Socket — for networking.

sections.title: Practice Questions — Test Your Packages & API Knowledge

blocks.text: Challenge yourself with these practice questions. Attempt each independently before reading the answer — writing and tracing code by hand significantly improves retention and interview readiness.

items.q: 1. A Java file is saved at src/com/example/util/StringHelper.java. What must the first executable statement in this file be?
items.a: The first executable statement must be: package com.example.util; — The package declaration must match the directory structure exactly (com/example/util/ → com.example.util). It must be the very first statement in the file — before any import statements, before any class declarations, and before any blank lines (though comments above it are technically allowed). If this statement is missing or incorrect, the Java compiler will report an error because the class's declared package does not match its physical location on disk.

Line 1 prints: false. 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly in IEEE 754 double precision. Their sum is approximately 0.30000000000000004, not exactly 0.3. The == comparison fails. Line 2 prints: 0. BigDecimal constructed from String represents values exactly. new BigDecimal("0.1").add(new BigDecimal("0.2")) is exactly 0.3. compareTo(new BigDecimal("0.3")) returns 0 (equal). Key lesson: never compare doubles with == for exact equality, especially in financial code. Always use BigDecimal (String constructor) for exact decimal arithmetic. compareTo() is correct for BigDecimal equality checks — equals() also checks scale (0.3 vs 0.30 are equals() false but compareTo() zero).

Line B causes a COMPILE ERROR: secret has no access modifier (package-private) — it is only visible within com.example.a. Class B is in com.example.b — a completely different package. Despite the apparent parent-child relationship of the package names, com.example.a and com.example.b are independent packages with no shared access. The compiler error: secret is not public in com.example.a.A; cannot be accessed from outside package. Fix: make secret public, or move class B into com.example.a.

items.q: 5. Using java.util, write a program that: creates a list of 5 student names, sorts them alphabetically, removes all names shorter than 4 characters, and prints the final list.

items.a: Three errors: Error 1: import java.util.ArrayList; comes BEFORE package com.example; — the package declaration must be the FIRST statement. The import must come after the package line. Error 2: BigDecimal is used but not imported. Need: import java.math.BigDecimal; Error 3: new BigDecimal(9.99) uses the double constructor — this inherits floating-point imprecision. 9.99 as a double is not exactly 9.99. Should use String constructor: new BigDecimal("9.99"). Additionally, ArrayList is imported but never used — a dead import (not a compile error, but an IDE warning and code smell). Fixed version: package com.example; import java.math.BigDecimal; public class MyApp { public static void main(String[] args) { BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("9.99"); } }

items.q: 7. Write a program using java.math.BigDecimal to calculate compound interest: P = 10000, rate = 8.5% per annum, time = 3 years. Formula: A = P * (1 + r)^n. Round to 2 decimal places.
8. How would you properly organize a simple e-commerce application into packages? Describe the package structure and what each package contains.
items.a:
Recommended package structure for an e-commerce app using layer-based organization:

com.ecommerce (root — holds only the main application entry point)
com.ecommerce.model — domain entities: Product, Order, Customer, Cart, Payment
com.ecommerce.service — business logic: ProductService, OrderService, PaymentService, CartService
com.ecommerce.repository — data access: ProductRepository, OrderRepository, CustomerRepository
com.ecommerce.controller — API endpoints / UI handlers: ProductController, OrderController
com.ecommerce.exception — custom exceptions: ProductNotFoundException, InsufficientStockException, PaymentFailedException
com.ecommerce.util — stateless helper classes: PriceCalculator, ValidationUtils, DateUtils
com.ecommerce.config — app configuration: DatabaseConfig, SecurityConfig

Principles applied: (1) Each package has a single clear responsibility. (2) Dependencies flow inward: controller → service → repository. (3) model classes have no package dependencies. (4) exception and util are shared cross-cutting packages. (5) Package-private visibility can hide repository implementation details from controller layer.

sections.title: Conclusion — Packages & API: Java's Organizational Backbone

blocks.text: Packages are not just a code organization tool — they are Java's fundamental namespace, visibility control, and architectural expression mechanism. Every professional Java codebase is a carefully designed package hierarchy that reflects the application's architecture, enforces encapsulation through access control, and prevents naming conflicts at scale. How you organize your packages reveals how clearly you understand your system's design.

The Java API — hundreds of packages and thousands of battle-tested classes — is one of Java's greatest strengths. Before writing any utility code, ask: does the Java API already have this? The answer is almost always yes. java.time for dates, java.math.BigDecimal for money, java.util for collections, java.nio.file for files — these are not optional libraries but core skills every Java developer must master. Knowing the API deeply is what separates a Java programmer from a Java developer.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Packages and API

items.q: What is a package in Java?
items.a: A package in Java is a namespace that groups related classes, interfaces, enumerations, and annotations together. It serves three purposes: organization (related types stored together), name collision prevention (same-named classes in different packages coexist), and access control (package-private visibility). Packages map directly to directory structure — com.example.service maps to com/example/service/ on disk. The package declaration must be the first statement in a Java source file. If omitted, the class belongs to the unnamed default package — acceptable for experiments, never for production code.

items.q: What is the Java API?
items.a: The Java API (Application Programming Interface) is the collection of pre-written packages and classes that ship with every Java installation as the Java Standard Library. It provides ready-to-use implementations for common tasks: data structures (java.util), I/O (java.io, java.nio), math (java.math), date/time (java.time), networking (java.net), concurrency (java.util.concurrent), and more. Before writing any utility code, always check if the Java API already provides it — it almost always does, and the built-in implementations are battle-tested, optimized, and well-documented.

items.q: Which package is automatically imported in Java?
items.a: java.lang is the only package automatically imported into every Java source file. It contains the most fundamental Java classes: String, Integer, Long, Double, Boolean, Math, Object, System, StringBuilder, Thread, Runnable, Exception, RuntimeException, NullPointerException, ArithmeticException, and all primitive wrapper classes. This is why you can use String and System.out.println() without any import statement. All other packages — including java.util, java.io, java.time, java.math, and every third-party library — must be explicitly imported.

items.q: Why should you use BigDecimal instead of double for money?
items.a: double uses IEEE 754 binary floating-point, which cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. 0.1 + 0.2 in double gives 0.30000000000000004 — not 0.3. In financial calculations, these tiny errors accumulate and produce wrong totals, taxes, and balances. java.math.BigDecimal represents decimals exactly. Always use the String constructor — new BigDecimal("19.99") is exact; new BigDecimal(19.99) inherits the double's imprecision. Always specify RoundingMode — HALF_UP for financial values. Never use double, float, or the double-based BigDecimal constructor for any monetary calculation.

items.q: What is the difference between package-private and private access in Java?
items.a: private restricts access to only the declaring class itself — no other class, not even other classes in the same package, can access private members. package-private (no modifier) allows access to any class in the same package, but blocks access from all other packages (including sub-packages). This distinction is important for encapsulation design: use private for members that are purely internal implementation of a single class. Use package-private for members that need to be shared within a module/package but should not be exposed as part of the public API. Sub-packages do NOT inherit package-private access — each package is completely isolated.
